On further thought (and beyond just the typo) I think there's merit to checking g_lastvblank < vblankrecieved and not doing the compare if it is. The last vblank itself is atomic, but there's no expectating of atomicity between the vblank timestamp getting updated and the message getting sent/handled.

So you could have a coincidental race where we happen to handle a message super late in the steamcompmgr side because we were blocked for a long time, and the vblankmanager has _just_ updated the timestamp for the next vblank and not sent the message yet. In this case we should draw twice and pull two frames, as we could handle the next event as well. Really we should be encoding that uint64_t into the two data members of our user event and remove that horrible hack from existence, now that you're encoding time in a more convenient way than a timespec. Right?

For this PR, we can just load `g_lastvblank` before getting `vblankrecieved` to fix the race.

Why char?

> Why char?

For some reason, you can't do `fetch_or` on a boolean atomic...
Which in the one case where I use it, I can't cleanly replace it with something like an atomic exchange.
only integral atomics can do stuff like `fetch_or`
https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/atomic/atomic#Specializations_for_integral_types
*(note that technically on x86_64, w/ how I grab the old value of the atomic when using `fetch_or`, `fetch_or` actually gets compiled into an [atomic compare exchange](https://preshing.com/20150402/you-can-do-any-kind-of-atomic-read-modify-write-operation/) (which is still lock-free)  because x86_64 `lock or` instruction does not return the old value of the atomic. Funnily enough, aarch64 and riscv [w/ the right atomic isa support] have their own version of `lock or` that actually returns the old value of the atomic.)*

So I use char, since a bool, when stored in a struct/class (in most implementations), actually occupies the same amount of memory as a char.
Would you prefer I use `uint8_t` instead of char?

I believe most modern cpus should support lock-free atomics on 8 bit values, so I think it should be fine?

I know that basically all x86_64 cpus support it,
plus the same aarch64 isa extension that provided support for stuff like atomic increment also gave support for operations on a wider variety of atomic sizes, including 8bit:
https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20220811-00/?p=106963

What actually washes the colors out is the HDR path. The panel's CTA block advertises BT2020RGB and ST2084, so without a script gamescope exposes HDR with PQ output encoding, and the session enables it immediately ("xwm: HDR output enabled"). The panel is natively gamma 2.2 per its own EDID, so PQ-encoded output looks washed out. The load-bearing line in the script is `eotf = gamescope.eotf.gamma22`, the same pattern as `valve.steamdeck.oled.lua` and `zotac.zone.oled.lua`. The luminance values are the EDID's own numbers restated.
